subsystems.name: Light-emitting cell payload
subsystems.role: living skin cells engineered to make a luciferase enzyme that emits photons.

subsystems.name: Substrate supply
subsystems.role: luciferase needs a chemical fuel; supplying it inside the body is the hardest part of the concept.
parts: bacterial lux operon genes for self-made substrate
or D-luciferin delivered topically or by injection

subsystems.name: Gene control circuit
subsystems.role: a glow you cannot switch on, dim or switch off is not a product.

subsystems.name: Delivery and integration
subsystems.role: gets the genes into skin cells and keeps them there.
parts: CRISPR-Cas9 knock-in at a safe genomic site
or ex vivo grafting of edited cells grown in the lab

subsystems.name: Optical placement
subsystems.role: where the tissue sits determines how much light actually escapes.
parts: epidermal placement under a thin keratin layer
avoidance of melanin-rich cells that absorb visible light

subsystems.name: Immune and tissue management
subsystems.role: engineered cells must survive in skin, which turns over and is immune-active.
parts: use of the patient's own cells to avoid rejection
immunosuppression protocols if donor cells are used

buildSteps.title: Choose the light chemistry
buildSteps.detail: Two routes exist: firefly luciferase, which needs an external substrate called D-luciferin and gives bright, well-understood light, or the bacterial lux operon from marine bacteria such as Vibrio fischeri, which makes its own substrate and so is self-sufficient but dimmer and harder to express in human cells.

buildSteps.title: Design the gene cassette
buildSteps.detail: The luciferase genes are codon-optimised for human cells, placed under an inducible promoter, and flanked by the sequences needed for targeted insertion. A safety switch that kills the cell if it misbehaves is added at the same time.

buildSteps.title: Edit the cells
buildSteps.detail: Working outside the body, CRISPR-Cas9 is used to insert the cassette into a chosen 'safe harbour' site in the genome of the patient's own skin cells, so the change is stable across cell divisions and does not disrupt a working gene.

buildSteps.title: Validate in culture
buildSteps.detail: The edited cells are grown in sheets, given substrate or nutrients, and their light output measured in a dark box with a sensitive camera. This is the point where the numbers get hard: emitting 1 lux over one square metre of skin is roughly 1.5 milliwatts of visible light, which is trivial for a cell, but a glow bright enough to read by in daylight needs watts, competing with the blood supply to the skin.

buildSteps.title: Test in animal skin
buildSteps.detail: Engineered human skin is grafted onto mice and imaged from outside. Luminescence imaging of this kind is already routine in research laboratories, but only as a measurement tool, not as a cosmetic glow.

buildSteps.title: Build a graft or delivery vehicle
buildSteps.detail: The cells are either grown into an epidermal sheet for grafting, sprayed on as a suspension, or the genes are delivered directly into existing skin with a vector. Delivery into the dermis, as fibroblasts sit there, scatters the light badly, so epidermal keratinocytes are the better target.

buildSteps.title: Run safety and immune studies
buildSteps.detail: Long-term checks for tumour formation, immune rejection, gene silencing and loss of the glow over months of skin turnover. Autologous cells avoid rejection but make the process slow and expensive per patient.

buildSteps.title: First human studies
buildSteps.detail: The realistic first use is medical, not aesthetic: a faint engineered glow that lets clinicians track whether a graft or engineered tissue has survived, replacing injections of imaging chemicals.

buildSteps.title: Product engineering
buildSteps.detail: Only once dimming, patterning, power supply and long-term stability work would a cosmetic overlay become a product — and the regulatory path for a permanent genetic change for appearance alone is far stricter than for a therapy.

prerequisites.why: makes stable, targeted insertion into human skin cells practical.
decades of use as laboratory imaging reporters prove the light-emitting chemistry works in living mammals.

prerequisites.tech: Self-sufficient substrate production in human cells
prerequisites.why: firefly luciferase needs an external chemical supply, and getting the bacterial self-supplying pathway to work well inside human cells is unresolved.

prerequisites.tech: Tunable inducible gene circuits in skin
prerequisites.why: simple switches work in cell culture and animal models, but stable, dose-controlled expression over years in human skin is not demonstrated.
skin gene therapies and cultured grafts exist, but prolonged expression of a foreign enzyme risks rejection or silencing.

pathway.milestone: luciferase reporter genes used routinely to image tumours and track cells in laboratory animals
pathway.unlocks: the measurement and genetic toolkit, in a research setting only.

pathway.milestone: engineered skin grafts carrying a reporter gene, used clinically to check that a graft has taken
pathway.unlocks: a legitimate medical use and the first regulatory precedent for light-emitting human tissue.

pathway.milestone: in vivo delivery to existing skin with an inducible, dimmable glow
pathway.unlocks: removal of surgery from the process and a test of long-term safety.

pathway.milestone: programmable, patterned, tunable emission across large skin areas
pathway.unlocks: the aesthetic product — if regulators ever accept permanent genetic modification for appearance, and if brightness can be achieved without harming the skin.
